item.title: Nara Sumi Ink and Calligraphy: The Craft of Black Ink — Guide
item.description: Nara is the historic heart of Japanese sumi ink-making, producing the great majority of the country’s traditional ink sticks (nara-zumi) for around 600 years. The craft is beautifully simple and painstaking: fine soot collected from burning oils or pine is kneaded with animal glue and fragrance, pressed in wooden moulds, and slowly dried over weeks into the solid ink sticks that are ground with water on a stone inkstone to make ink for calligraphy and painting.

item.title: Yoshino Woodworking and Kumiko: Craft of the Cedar Forests — Guide
item.description: The mountains of Yoshino are famed not only for cherry blossoms but for their forests: Yoshino cedar (sugi) and cypress (hinoki), grown for centuries in one of Japan’s oldest managed plantations, are prized as some of the finest timber in the country, used for everything from temple beams to sake barrels. From this woodworking heritage comes kumiko, the delicate craft of assembling tiny wooden pieces into intricate geometric latticework without nails, traditionally used in shoji screens and transoms.

item.title: Echizen Pottery: One of Japan's Six Ancient Kilns — Guide
item.description: Echizen ware is one of Japan’s Six Ancient Kilns, the country’s most historically significant pottery-producing centres, with a ceramic tradition in the region spanning some 850 years, known for its unglazed, earthy, high-fired stoneware whose natural ash-glaze finishes develop during wood firing. Today the Echizen pottery area gathers kilns, galleries and a ceramic museum, and workshops let visitors try the potter’s wheel or hand-forming themselves under artisan guidance, shaping a piece to be fired and sent on later.

item.title: Wajima Lacquerware: One of Japan's Most Prized Lacquer Traditions — Guide
item.description: Wajima-nuri, the lacquerware produced in and around Wajima on the Noto Peninsula, is considered one of Japan’s most prized lacquer traditions, renowned for its exceptional durability achieved through a painstaking application process that can involve well over 100 individual steps, including a distinctive undercoat reinforced with diatomaceous earth and cloth to strengthen the finished piece against daily wear. Visitors can try hands-on workshops in Wajima, working under artisan guidance to decorate or finish a small lacquerware piece, offering a hands-on introduction to a craft that traditionally takes years of apprenticeship to master.

item.title: Aizu Lacquerware Painting Workshop: A 400-Year Craft Tradition — Guide
item.description: Aizu-nuri lacquerware is one of Japan’s foremost lacquerware traditions, dating back over 400 years to when a feudal lord invited lacquer artisans to Aizu to develop the local craft as an economic industry. The result is a distinctive style known for its warm gold and vermillion maki-e decoration, and today, workshops throughout Aizu-Wakamatsu let visitors try their hand at painting a small lacquerware piece — such as a bowl, chopsticks or small box — under the guidance of trained artisans, taking home a genuinely handmade souvenir.
